{{Short description|Skew polygon derived from a polytope}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
{{multiple image
 | align = right  | total_width = 500
 | image1 = Skeleton 12, Petrie, stick, size l.png
 | image2 = Skeleton 12, Petrie, stick, size l, 5-fold.png
 | footer = The Petrie polygon of the [[regular dodecahedron|dodecahedron]] is a [[skew polygon|skew]] [[decagon]]. Seen from the solid's 5-fold symmetry axis it looks like a regular decagon. Every pair of consecutive sides belongs to one pentagon (but no triple does).
}}

In [[geometry]], a '''Petrie polygon''' for a [[regular polytope]] of {{mvar|n}} dimensions is a [[skew polygon]] in which every {{math|''n'' – 1}} consecutive [[Edge (geometry)|sides]] (but no {{mvar|n}}) belongs to one of the [[Facet (geometry)|facet]]s.  The '''Petrie polygon''' of a [[regular polygon]] is the regular polygon itself; that of a [[regular polyhedron]] is a skew polygon such that every two consecutive sides (but no three) belongs to one of the [[Face (geometry)|face]]s.<ref>'''Kaleidoscopes: Selected Writings of H. S. M. Coxeter''', edited by F. Arthur Sherk, [[Peter McMullen]], Anthony C. Thompson, Asia Ivić Weiss, Wiley-Interscience Publication, 1995, [https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Kaleidoscopes-p-9780471010036 wiley.com], {{isbn|978-0-471-01003-6}} (Definition: paper 13, Discrete groups generated by reflections, 1933, p. 161)</ref> Petrie polygons are named for mathematician [[John Flinders Petrie]].

For every regular polytope there exists an [[orthogonal projection]] onto a plane such that one Petrie polygon becomes a regular polygon with the remainder of the projection interior to it. The plane in question is the [[Coxeter plane]] of the [[symmetry group]] of the polygon, and the number of sides, {{mvar|h}}, is the [[Coxeter number]] of the [[Coxeter group]]. These polygons and projected graphs are useful in visualizing symmetric structure of the higher-dimensional regular polytopes.

Petrie polygons can be defined more generally for any [[Graph embedding|embedded graph]]. They form the faces of another embedding of the same graph, usually on a different surface, called the [[Petrie dual]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Pisanski | first1 = Tomaž | author1-link = Tomaž Pisanski
 | last2 = Randić | first2 = Milan | author2-link = Milan Randić
 | editor-last = Gorini | editor-first = Catherine A.
 | contribution = Bridges between geometry and graph theory
 | location = Washington, DC
 | mr = 1782654
 | pages = 174–194
 | publisher = Math. Assoc. America
 | series = MAA Notes
 | title = Geometry at work
 | volume = 53
 | year = 2000}}. See in particular [https://books.google.com/books?id=Eb6uSLa2k6IC&pg=PA181 p.&nbsp;181].</ref>
== History ==
John Flinders Petrie (1907–1972) was the son of [[Egyptologist]]s [[Hilda Petrie|Hilda]] and [[Sir W. M. Flinders Petrie|Flinders Petrie]]. He was born in 1907 and as a schoolboy showed remarkable promise of mathematical ability. In periods of intense concentration he could answer questions about complicated four-dimensional objects by ''visualizing'' them.

He first noted the importance of the regular skew polygons which appear on the surface of regular polyhedra and higher polytopes.  Coxeter explained in 1937 how he and Petrie began to expand the classical subject of regular polyhedra:
:One day in 1926, J. F. Petrie told me with much excitement that he had discovered two new regular polyhedral; infinite but free of false vertices. When my incredulity had begun to subside, he described them to me: one consisting of squares, six at each vertex, and one consisting of hexagons, four at each vertex.<ref>H.S.M. Coxeter (1937) "Regular skew polyhedral in three and four dimensions and their topological analogues", [[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]] (2) 43: 33 to 62</ref>
In 1938 Petrie collaborated with Coxeter, [[Patrick du Val]], and H. T. Flather to produce ''[[The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra]]'' for publication.<ref>H. S. M. Coxeter, [[Patrick du Val]], H. T. Flather, J. F. Petrie (1938) ''The Fifty-nine Icosahedra'', [[University of Toronto]] studies, mathematical series 6: 1–26</ref>
Realizing the geometric facility of the skew polygons used by Petrie, Coxeter named them after his friend when he wrote ''[[Regular Polytopes]]''.

The idea of Petrie polygons was later extended to [[semiregular polytope]]s.

The [[dual polyhedron|regular duals]], {''p'',''q''} and {''q'',''p''}, are contained within the same projected Petrie polygon.
In the images of [[dual compound]]s on the right it can be seen that their Petrie polygons have rectangular intersections in the points where the edges touch the common [[midsphere]].

The Petrie polygons are the exterior of these orthogonal projections.<br />
The concentric rings of vertices are counted starting from the outside working inwards with a notation: ''V'':(''a'',&nbsp;''b'',&nbsp;...), ending in zero if there are no central vertices.<br />
The number of sides for {''p'',&nbsp;''q''} is 24/(10&nbsp;−&nbsp;''p''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''q'')&nbsp;−&nbsp;2.<ref>{{citation

 | title = On the number of sides of a Petrie polygon
 | volume = 10
 | year = 1958}}</ref>
|}

Infinite regular skew polygons ([[apeirogon]]) can also be defined as being the Petrie polygons of the regular tilings, having angles of 90, 120, and 60 degrees of their square, hexagon and triangular faces respectively.
:[[File:petrie_polygons_of_regular_tilings.png|720px|class=skin-invert]]

Infinite regular skew polygons also exist as Petrie polygons of the regular hyperbolic tilings, like the [[order-7 triangular tiling]], {3,7}:
:[[File:Order-7 triangular tiling petrie polygon.png|240px]]

== The Petrie polygon of regular polychora (4-polytopes) ==
{{multiple image
 | align = right | total_width = 500
 | image1 = Tesseract Schlegel Petrie.png
 | image2 = Numbered 4-cube.svg
 | footer = The Petrie polygon of the [[tesseract]] is an [[octagon]]. Every triple of consecutive sides belongs to one of its eight cubic cells.
}}

The Petrie polygon for the regular polychora {''p'',&nbsp;''q''&nbsp;,''r''} can also be determined, such that every three consecutive sides (but no four) belong to one of the polychoron's cells. As the surface of a 4-polytope is a 3-dimensional space (the [[3-sphere]]), the Petrie polygon of a regular 4-polytope is a 3-dimensional helix in this surface.

== The Petrie polygon projections of regular and uniform polytopes ==

The Petrie polygon projections are useful for the visualization of polytopes of dimension four and higher.

=== Hypercubes ===
A [[hypercube]] of dimension ''n'' has a Petrie polygon of size 2''n'', which is also the number of its [[Facet (geometry)|facets]].<br />
So each of the (''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)-cubes forming its [[hypersurface|surface]] has ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 sides of the Petrie polygon among its edges.
{| class="wikitable collapsible collapsed skin-invert" style="text-align: center;"
!colspan="3"| Hypercubes
|-
|colspan="3" style="text-align: left;"|
<small>The 1-cubes's Petrie [[digon]] looks identical to the 1-cube. But the 1-cube has a single edge, while the digon has two.<br /></small>
The 2-cube's Petrie square is identical to the 2-cube.<br />
Each pair of consecutive sides of the 3-cube's Petrie hexagon belongs to one of its six square faces.<br />
Each triple of consecutive sides of the 4-cube's Petrie octagon belongs to one of its eight cube cells.

The images show how the Petrie polygon for dimension ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 can be constructed from that for dimension&nbsp;''n'':
* The first half <small>(edges between vertices with numbers <&nbsp;2<sup>''n''</sup>)</small> remains where it is.
* The second half is moved to the next dimension <small>(2<sup>''n''</sup> added to vertex numbers)</small>.
* Two new edges <small>(shown in orange)</small> are added to connect the two parts.
<small>(For ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 the first and the second half are the two distinct but coinciding edges of a digon.)</small>

The sides of each Petrie polygon belong to these dimensions:<br />
({{color|orange|1}}, {{color|orange|1}}), &nbsp;
({{color|red|1}}, {{color|orange|2}}, {{color|red|1}}, {{color|orange|2}}), &nbsp;
({{color|red|1}}, {{color|red|2}}, {{color|orange|3}}, {{color|red|1}}, {{color|red|2}}, {{color|orange|3}}), &nbsp;
({{color|red|1}}, {{color|red|2}}, {{color|red|3}}, {{color|orange|4}}, {{color|red|1}}, {{color|red|2}}, {{color|red|3}}, {{color|orange|4}}), &nbsp; etc.<br />
So any ''n'' consecutive sides belong to different dimensions.
